claims.text: Homogeneous noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles require nearly simultaneous reduction of all metal precursors.
An ultrafast thermal pulse synchronizes reduction of the noble-metal precursors.
Synchronized precursor reduction causes rapid, simultaneous nucleation into unified multimetal clusters.
Rapid unified nucleation kinetically traps the metals before diffusion-driven phase separation or elemental segregation can occur.
Sequential or element-by-element nucleation during longer heating can cause phase separation, elemental segregation, or morphological irregularity.
Synchrony of metal-ion reduction leads to a single-phase alloy structure.
Sub-second pulse synthesis will produce more compositionally uniform, single-phase nanoparticles than conventional prolonged heating.
Nanoparticles produced by the ultrafast pulse will have high surface-atom exposure.
Prolonged heating will produce phase separation or compositional inhomogeneity relative to pulse heating.
Reduction of the individual metal ions will be more synchronized under the ultrafast pulse than under the baseline heating profile.
Conventional extended heating permits a wider, less synchronized reduction window and heterogeneous nucleation.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily when the precursors have comparable reduction potentials and similar ligand environments.
Large precursor-chemistry differences or local temperature gradients can create reduction-rate disparities that an ultrafast pulse cannot overcome.
The controlled comparison keeps precursor concentrations, polyol medium, and inert atmosphere identical between synthesis conditions.

contradictions.description: The conditions field says that both the thermal profile and simultaneous kinetic monitoring differ between groups, whereas the falsification design indicates that both groups are monitored in parallel. It is therefore unclear whether monitoring is a controlled measurement or an additional treatment difference.

The causal hypothesis predicts that achieved reduction synchrony should yield improved homogeneity, but the stated falsification rule requires both failure of synchrony and failure of structural improvement. Thus, synchronized reduction without improved homogeneity—an outcome that would directly challenge the proposed causal link—is not declared falsifying.
